title: Who gets a say
subtitle: Parental responsibility: who has it, how it is acquired, and what it actually confers
objectives: State who acquires parental responsibility automatically, and who must acquire it through a separate legal step
Identify the three routes by which an unmarried father (and the equivalent routes for step-parents and adopters) can acquire parental responsibility otherwise than automatically
Explain what parental responsibility does and does not confer, and distinguish it from other markers of a parent-child relationship such as biological parentage or day-to-day care

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines who has parental responsibility automatically, and how it can be shared
Defines what parental responsibility actually consists of
Sets out the routes by which an unmarried father acquires parental responsibility — registration, agreement, or court order

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often conflate 'being a parent' with 'having parental responsibility' — they are not the same thing, and the gap between them is where most exam marks in this topic are won or lost. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can probably list who has parental responsibility — this lesson checks whether you can spot who does NOT, on a given set of facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards working out, from a fact pattern, exactly who holds parental responsibility and who is missing it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about the automatic categories before moving on — everything else in this lesson assumes you know exactly who is, and isn't, covered by s 2.

overview.hook: A father who has never married the mother of his child, whose name is on the birth certificate, who sees his son every week and pays towards his upbringing, can still lack the legal power to consent to that child's medical treatment or agree which school he attends. Not because he isn't a parent in every ordinary sense of the word — but because 'parent' and 'parental responsibility' are two different legal ideas, and English law only ever asks about the second one when it comes to who can actually make decisions for a child.

parts.heading: Parental responsibility is not the same thing as being a parent
parts.voice: argumentative — separates a legal concept from an everyday one before building the detail
body: 'Parental responsibility' (PR) is a specific, defined legal status under the Children Act 1989 — not a general description of who a child's parents are, and not a reward for good parenting. A person can be a child's biological parent and lack parental responsibility entirely; conversely, a person with no biological connection to a child at all — a step-parent, an adopter, sometimes even a local authority — can hold it.

Why does the distinction matter this much? Because parental responsibility is the legal key that unlocks the ability to make decisions for a child: consenting to medical treatment, choosing or changing a school, agreeing to a change of surname, consenting to the child's marriage where relevant, and being consulted (though not necessarily agreeing) on major life decisions. Someone without it is not, in the law's eyes, in a position to exercise any of that authority — however closely involved they are in the child's life day to day.

This lesson maps who gets parental responsibility automatically, on the basis of status alone, and who has to actively acquire it through one of several defined legal routes. The split is not random, and it is not (any longer) explicitly tied to gender — but it is still tied to marital status in a way that produces real, sometimes surprising, gaps.

components.definition: Under s 3 Children Act 1989: all the rights, duties, powers, responsibilities and authority which by law a parent of a child has in relation to the child and his property. It is a defined legal status, separate from biological parenthood, that can be held by more than one person at once and does not automatically follow from being a child's genetic or gestational parent.

interaction.prompt: Is it possible for a child's biological father to lack parental responsibility?
options: Yes — biological parenthood alone does not automatically confer parental responsibility on a father
No — every biological parent automatically has parental responsibility
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Biological fatherhood and parental responsibility are separate concepts; whether an unmarried father has PR depends on which of the routes in Part 3 he has used, not on genetics alone.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Biological parenthood on its own is not enough for a father outside the automatic categories — that gap, and the routes that close it, are exactly what this lesson covers.

parts.heading: The automatic categories
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Two categories of person acquire parental responsibility automatically, by operation of law, with no separate application needed. The birth mother always has parental responsibility from the moment of birth — this is the one category with no exceptions and no route required, whatever her marital status. Whoever else is married to, or in a civil partnership with, the mother at the time of the child's birth also acquires parental responsibility automatically, whether or not they are the child's biological parent — a consequence of the marital presumption running through this whole area of law.

This means a husband is treated as having parental responsibility for a child born to his wife during the marriage, even before any question of biological paternity is raised — and even if it later turns out he is not the biological father, though that can affect other things (child arrangements, maintenance liability) separately. The automatic-acquisition rule is about status at the time of birth, not about genetic testing.

Everyone else — an unmarried father, a step-parent, an adopter before the adoption order, a same-sex second parent outside the automatic categories under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008 — starts without parental responsibility and must acquire it through one of the routes covered in Parts 3 and 4.

components.label: Who has parental responsibility automatically
points: The birth mother — always, from birth, regardless of marital status
A person married to, or in civil partnership with, the mother at the time of birth — automatically, regardless of biological connection
Everyone else (unmarried fathers, step-parents, adopters, some second parents) must acquire it separately

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether the mother's husband automatically has parental responsibility for the child.
interaction.scenarioText: Amara gives birth to a son. She has been married to Ben for three years, though the couple have been separated (but not divorced) for the last eight months, and the child was in fact conceived with a different partner. Ben is still legally married to Amara at the date of the birth.
tappableSpans: married to Ben for three years
separated (but not divorced) for the last eight months
Ben is still legally married to Amara at the date of the birth
interaction.correctSpan: Ben is still legally married to Amara at the date of the birth
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the trigger. Automatic acquisition turns on marital status at the moment of birth, not on biological paternity or on whether the couple are currently living together — Ben has parental responsibility automatically because he is Amara's husband when the child is born.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Separation and biological parentage are both distractions here — the rule is purely about legal marital status at the date of birth. Ben's continuing marriage to Amara at that moment is what matters.

parts.heading: The three routes for an unmarried father
body: An unmarried father — not married to, and not in civil partnership with, the mother at the time of birth — does not get parental responsibility automatically. Section 4 Children Act 1989 gives him three separate routes to acquire it, any one of which is sufficient on its own.

The most common route today is registration: being jointly registered as the child's father on the birth certificate, since a change introduced in December 2003, itself confers parental responsibility. This is why the date of the child's birth registration, and whether the father was named on it, is often the first question to ask in an exam problem about an unmarried father's status. Before that change, joint registration alone did not confer PR — which is why very old fact patterns (children born before December 2003) can produce a different answer, though this is now a rare wrinkle.

The second route is a parental responsibility agreement — a formal, prescribed-form agreement between the mother and father, which must be filed at court to take effect; a private, informal understanding between the parents is not enough. The third route is a parental responsibility order, which the father can apply for from the court where the mother does not agree, and which the court grants having regard to the child's welfare — commitment shown to the child, the degree of attachment, and the father's reasons for applying are all relevant factors the courts have weighed in this context.

components.text: Where a child's father and mother were not married to, or civil partners of, each other at the time of his birth, the father shall acquire parental responsibility for the child if— (a) he becomes registered as the child's father...; (b) he and the child's mother make an agreement (a 'parental responsibility agreement') providing for him to have parental responsibility for the child; or (c) the court, on his application, orders that he shall have parental responsibility for the child.
elements: Registration as the child's father on the birth certificate
A formal parental responsibility agreement in the prescribed form, filed at court
A parental responsibility order made by the court on the father's application

interaction.prompt: An unmarried father and mother cannot agree on parental responsibility. Put the realistic sequence of what he would need to do in order, starting from the point where informal registration is not available to him.
items: He is not registered as the child's father on the birth certificate
He proposes a parental responsibility agreement, but the mother refuses to sign it
He applies to the court for a parental responsibility order under s 4(1)(c)
The court decides the application having regard to the child's welfare
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the realistic escalation: registration first (if available), then a negotiated agreement, and only once both of those are unavailable or refused does a court application become necessary.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about which routes require the mother's cooperation and which don't. Registration and agreement both need her involvement; only the court order route under s 4(1)(c) is available to a father acting entirely unilaterally when she won't cooperate.

parts.heading: Step-parents and adopters: acquiring PR without a biological link
parts.voice: structural — extends the routes beyond the birth-father case
body: Parental responsibility is not limited to biological parents at all. A step-parent — married to, or in civil partnership with, a parent who already has parental responsibility — can acquire parental responsibility for their stepchild in essentially the same three ways an unmarried father can: by parental responsibility agreement with every person who already has parental responsibility for the child, or by a parental responsibility order from the court under s 4A Children Act 1989. Marriage to the child's parent, by itself, is not enough — the step-parent must take one of these additional steps.

Adoption works differently, and more completely: an adoption order under the Adoption and Children Act 2002 extinguishes the parental responsibility of the child's birth parents (subject to very limited exceptions) and vests parental responsibility exclusively in the adopters, as if the child had been born to them. This is the one route that displaces existing holders of parental responsibility rather than simply adding to them — which is why adoption is treated, throughout this module, as the most legally final of all the routes into a parent-child relationship.

A useful habit for exam answers: whenever a fact pattern introduces someone other than a birth parent — a step-parent, a grandparent raising a child, a same-sex second parent outside the automatic HFEA 2008 categories — the first question is always 'has this person taken one of the defined steps to acquire parental responsibility,' not 'do they behave like a parent.'

components.label: Acquiring parental responsibility without automatic entitlement
points: Unmarried father — registration, agreement, or court order (s 4)
Step-parent — agreement with existing PR holders, or court order (s 4A)
Adopter — an adoption order under the Adoption and Children Act 2002, which also extinguishes the birth parents' parental responsibility
In every route except adoption, acquiring parental responsibility adds a holder rather than removing an existing one

interaction.prompt: Which of these two people has acquired parental responsibility purely by marrying a parent, with no further step taken?
interaction.scenarioA: Tomasz marries Ela, who has an eight-year-old daughter from a previous relationship. He has not entered any parental responsibility agreement or applied to court.
interaction.scenarioB: Fatima marries Yusuf, who has a ten-year-old son. She later enters a formal parental responsibility agreement with Yusuf and the child's other parent, filed at court.
interaction.explanation: Neither has parental responsibility purely by marriage — but the scenario is testing whether you recognise that Tomasz has taken no further step at all, so he has none, while Fatima has correctly completed the s 4A agreement route and does hold parental responsibility.

parts.heading: What parental responsibility does — and does not — give you
parts.voice: direct — closes by defining the boundaries of the status, not just who holds it
body: Parental responsibility gives its holder the legal authority to make (or share in making) decisions about a child's upbringing: consent to medical treatment, choice of school, consent to a change of name, religious upbringing, and consent to taking the child abroad, among others. Where more than one person holds parental responsibility — commonly both parents — each can, in principle, act alone to exercise it in respect of most day-to-day matters, though certain significant decisions (changing a child's surname, or removing the child permanently from the jurisdiction) require the consent of everyone with parental responsibility or a court order.

What it does not give you is automatic day-to-day care of the child, a right to a particular child arrangements order, or any say over who the child lives with as a matter of entitlement — those are separate questions, governed by s 8 child arrangements orders and the welfare principle covered in the next lesson. Parental responsibility is about legal decision-making authority, not physical custody or contact, and a person can hold parental responsibility while a child lives full-time with someone else.

It is also worth being precise that parental responsibility does not create any inheritance right, does not by itself determine financial liability for the child's maintenance (governed separately by the Child Maintenance Service framework and, in limited cases, Schedule 1 claims), and can, in rare and serious cases, be removed or restricted by a court where a holder poses a risk to the child — though courts are cautious about doing so, given how significant a step removing PR entirely is.

components.title: What PR governs versus what it doesn't
components.description: A quick map of the boundary between parental responsibility and other legal questions about a child.

nodes.label: Governs: choice of school, religious upbringing
Governs: consent to change of name / removal from jurisdiction (jointly, or with court leave)
Does NOT govern: who the child lives with day to day
Does NOT govern: financial maintenance liability

components.textAlternative: Parental responsibility governs consent to medical treatment, choice of school and religious upbringing, and (jointly, or with court leave) consent to a change of name or removal of the child from the jurisdiction. It does not govern who the child lives with day to day (a separate child arrangements question), financial maintenance liability, or inheritance rights.

interaction.prompt: A father with parental responsibility lives apart from his son, who lives full-time with the mother. The father wants to know whether his parental responsibility gives him the right to have the child live with him instead. Analyse his position.
factsToOrder: The child currently lives full-time with the mother
The father wants the child to live with him instead

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether holding parental responsibility entitles the father to have the child live with him.
modelAnswer.rule: Parental responsibility confers legal decision-making authority (s 3 Children Act 1989) but does not itself determine where a child lives; that question is governed separately by a child arrangements order under s 8, decided by reference to the welfare principle.
modelAnswer.application: The father's parental responsibility gives him a voice in decisions such as medical treatment or schooling, and standing to apply for a child arrangements order, but it does not by itself entitle him to have the child live with him — that outcome would require a separate application, assessed against the child's welfare, not against who holds parental responsibility.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Parental responsibility alone gives the father no automatic right to have the child live with him; he would need to apply for a child arrangements order, to be decided on the welfare principle.

testPool.prompt: Name the two categories of person who acquire parental responsibility automatically at a child's birth.
acceptableAnswers: the birth mother, and the person married to or in civil partnership with her at birth
birth mother and her spouse/civil partner at the time of birth
testPool.modelAnswer: The birth mother, always; and whoever is married to or in civil partnership with the mother at the time of the child's birth, regardless of biological connection.

testPool.prompt: Does being named on a child's birth certificate as the father, on its own, confer parental responsibility on an unmarried father registered since December 2003?
options: Yes — joint registration since December 2003 is itself one of the s 4 routes to parental responsibility
No — the father must always additionally obtain a court order

testPool.prompt: Which of the following does NOT, by itself, give a step-parent parental responsibility for their stepchild?
options: A parental responsibility agreement under s 4A with existing holders of parental responsibility
A parental responsibility order from the court under s 4A
Marrying the child's parent
testPool.trapExplanation: Marriage to the parent, by itself, does not confer parental responsibility on a step-parent — an additional step (agreement or court order) is always required, unlike the automatic acquisition rule that applies to a spouse who is present at the time of the child's birth.

testPool.prompt: Put these routes to parental responsibility for an unmarried father in the order s 4 Children Act 1989 lists them.
items: A parental responsibility agreement with the mother
A parental responsibility order from the court

testPool.prompt: According to s 4(1) Children Act 1989, what must a parental responsibility agreement do to be effective, beyond the parents simply agreeing between themselves?
options: Nothing further — an oral agreement between the parents is sufficient
It must be made in the prescribed form and filed at court
It must be approved by a local authority social worker

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that explains why adoption is treated as more legally final than the other routes to parental responsibility.
testPool.passage: Most routes to parental responsibility — registration, agreement, or a court order — simply add a new holder alongside those who already have it. Adoption is different: an adoption order under the Adoption and Children Act 2002 extinguishes the parental responsibility of the birth parents, subject to very limited exceptions, and vests it exclusively in the adopters, as if the child had been born to them.
testPool.ratioSentence: Adoption is different: an adoption order under the Adoption and Children Act 2002 extinguishes the parental responsibility of the birth parents, subject to very limited exceptions, and vests it exclusively in the adopters, as if the child had been born to them.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this unmarried father does NOT yet have parental responsibility.
testPool.scenarioText: Daniel is the biological father of a daughter born in 2024. He was not married to the mother at the time of birth. He was not registered as the father on the birth certificate, he and the mother never signed a parental responsibility agreement, and he has not applied to the court for a parental responsibility order.
tappableSpans: was not registered as the father on the birth certificate
he and the mother never signed a parental responsibility agreement
has not applied to the court for a parental responsibility order
testPool.correctSpan: has not applied to the court for a parental responsibility order
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — any one of the three s 4 routes would be enough, so the fact that none of the three (including the court order route) has been used is what confirms Daniel lacks parental responsibility. Biological fatherhood alone was never going to be enough.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: All three routes matter, but the decisive fact is that none of them — including the court order route, the one available even without the mother's cooperation — has been taken up. Biological fatherhood alone never confers parental responsibility on an unmarried father.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario shows a person who has parental responsibility without any biological connection to the child?
testPool.scenarioA: A husband who is married to the child's mother at the time of birth, but is later shown by DNA testing not to be the biological father, and has never taken any further legal step.
testPool.scenarioB: A biological father who was never married to the mother, was not registered on the birth certificate, and has taken no other step under s 4.
testPool.explanation: A shows automatic acquisition by marital status at birth, entirely independent of biology — the husband keeps parental responsibility even once biological paternity is disproved, unless a court removes it. B is the mirror case: a biological connection with no legal step taken produces no parental responsibility at all.

testPool.prompt: A mother wants to take her ten-year-old child to live permanently in another country. The child's father has parental responsibility but they were never married. What does the father's parental responsibility allow him to do about this?
options: Nothing — parental responsibility only concerns medical and educational decisions
His consent (or a court order in its place) is generally required before the child can be permanently relocated out of the jurisdiction
He can prevent the move only if he is named on the birth certificate, regardless of whether he has parental responsibility
testPool.explanation: Permanent relocation abroad is one of the significant decisions requiring the consent of everyone with parental responsibility, or the leave of the court in its absence — the father's consent (however he acquired parental responsibility) is legally relevant here, not merely birth-certificate registration on its own.

testPool.prompt: Marek and Nina were never married. Nina is the birth mother. Marek was not registered on the birth certificate at the time (registration predates December 2003 for this child), and he and Nina never signed an agreement. Marek has, however, been closely involved in the child's life for years and now wishes to be consulted on which secondary school the child attends. Analyse whether Marek currently has the legal standing to be involved in that decision.
factsToOrder: Marek and Nina were never married
Marek was not registered as the father on the birth certificate
No parental responsibility agreement was ever signed
Marek has been closely involved in the child's life
Marek wants a say in the choice of secondary school

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Marek has the legal standing to be involved in a decision about the child's schooling.
modelAnswer.rule: Only a person with parental responsibility (s 3 Children Act 1989) has the legal authority to be involved in such decisions. An unmarried father acquires it via registration, agreement, or court order (s 4); involvement in the child's life, however genuine, is not itself one of those routes, though it is a relevant factor if he applies for a court order.
modelAnswer.application: None of the three s 4 routes has been completed: no registration conferring PR, no signed agreement, and no order has been sought. His close involvement in the child's life does not itself confer parental responsibility, though it would likely support an application for a parental responsibility order if he made one.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Marek does not currently have the legal standing to be involved in the schooling decision; he would need to obtain parental responsibility through an agreement with Nina or, if she does not agree, a court order, before he has any legal say.

testPool.prompt: Which statement about what parental responsibility confers is correct?
options: Parental responsibility automatically determines which parent the child lives with day to day
Parental responsibility confers legal decision-making authority over matters such as medical treatment and education, but does not itself decide where the child lives
Parental responsibility automatically entitles its holder to child maintenance payments
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers conflate parental responsibility with living arrangements or with the separate maintenance system. Parental responsibility is specifically about legal decision-making authority under s 3, not physical custody or money.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that more than one person can hold parental responsibility for the same child at the same time?
sliderLabels: Not confident — only one person can hold it
Confident — several people can hold it simultaneously
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — several people can hold it simultaneously
testPool.explanation: Correct: parental responsibility is not exclusive. Both parents, and potentially a step-parent or adopter too, can hold it at the same time — acquiring it typically adds a holder rather than displacing an existing one, except on adoption.

testPool.prompt: A grandmother provides most of the day-to-day care for her grandchild but has taken no formal legal step to acquire parental responsibility, while a same-sex spouse of the birth mother was married to her at the time of the child's birth. Applying s 2 and the HFEA 2008 provisions on legal parenthood, which of the two holds parental responsibility?
options: The same-sex spouse, by automatic acquisition through her status at the time of birth
The grandmother, because day-to-day care is itself sufficient to confer parental responsibility
Neither, because parental responsibility can only be acquired by a biological parent
testPool.explanation: The spouse falls within the automatic-acquisition principle for a spouse/civil partner present at birth. The grandmother's devoted caregiving does not confer parental responsibility without a formal step being taken — day-to-day care is not itself a route to legal parental responsibility.

testPool.prompt: An unmarried father applies to the court for a parental responsibility order because the mother refuses to agree. What does the court primarily have regard to in deciding the application?
options: The child's welfare, including factors such as the father's degree of commitment and attachment to the child
Whether the father earns enough to support the child financially
Whether the mother consents, which is determinative
testPool.explanation: The mother's refusal to agree is precisely why the s 4(1)(c) court route exists — her consent is not determinative. The court decides by reference to the child's welfare, weighing factors like the father's commitment, attachment, and his reasons for applying.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming biological parenthood, marriage to a parent, or close day-to-day involvement automatically confers parental responsibility. Outside the two automatic categories in s 2, parental responsibility must always be actively acquired through one of the defined statutory routes.
